source: Svante Janson 2014, Tibetan calendar mathematics, arXiv:1401.6285v1

source_notes.paraphrase: Traditional day boundary is theoretical mean dawn, near 05:00 local mean solar; source says no physical sunrise calculation is required.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: A civil day takes the lunar-day label ending on it; skipped/repeated labels arise from timing differences.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: The mean lunar date is affine in true-month count and lunar-day count, with distinct rational month/day rates and epoch constants.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Mean Sun is linear in month/day counts and uses a separate mixed radix with 67 as final place, not the calendar time radix 707.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Moon anomaly has a source-used rounded lunar-day increment and a more exact increment associated with Dharmashri/Henning; the source describes both.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: The Moon correction interpolates a specified eight-sample signed-symmetry table over a 28-step cycle.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Sun correction uses a four-sample 12-step interpolation table; the corrected tithi-end time is mean date plus Moon minus Sun corrections divided by sixty.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Integer part of corrected tithi-end date gives the second day of a repeated number; first extra day precedes it, while same-day tithi endings create skipped labels.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Month begins on the day after the preceding true month's thirtieth lunar-day end; use this even if day one itself is skipped or doubled.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Losar is one civil day after day30 of preceding year's regular twelfth month, including when new month one is a leap month.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Weekday is (calendar JDN plus two) modulo seven, with Saturday assigned index zero.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study

source_notes.paraphrase: Tsurphu shares mean motion constants with Phugpa but has different epoch fractions, intercalation indices and floor-based month counts.
source_notes.source_kind: modern mathematical reconstruction, not original Tibetan source or prediction study
